title: Power and energy bills
description: Animated KS3 Physics lesson on power and energy bills for ages 9 to 14: watts and kilowatts, energy = power × time, kilowatt-hours, working out the cost of electricity, meter readings and saving energy.
intro: Watts, kilowatt-hours, electricity meters and what energy costs, explained by the owl in five short parts.

steps.say: Every electrical device has a **power**. Power tells you how **fast** a device transfers energy.
Power is measured in **watts**, written **W**. 1 W means 1 J of energy is transferred every second.
steps.speak: Power is measured in watts, written W. 1 watt means 1 joule of energy is transferred every second.

steps.say: A 10 W LED bulb transfers 10 J every second. A 60 W bulb transfers 60 J every second, so it uses energy six times as fast.
steps.speak: A 10 watt LED bulb transfers 10 joules every second. A 60 watt bulb transfers 60 joules every second, so it uses energy six times as fast.

steps.say: Big powers are written in **kilowatts**, **kW**. Kilo means a thousand, so 1 kW = 1000 W. A 2000 W kettle is a 2 kW kettle.
steps.speak: Big powers are written in kilowatts. Kilo means a thousand, so 1 kilowatt equals 1000 watts. A 2000 watt kettle is a 2 kilowatt kettle.

check.q: A heater has a power of 2000 W. How much energy does it transfer every second?
check.hint: 1 W means 1 J every second. So how many joules does 2000 W mean?
check.explain: Power in watts tells you the joules every second. 2000 W means **2000 J** every second. (2000 W is the same as 2 kW, but that is still 2000 J each second, not 2 J.)

steps.say: To work out the energy transferred: **energy = power × time**. Power in watts × time in seconds gives energy in joules.
steps.speak: To work out the energy transferred: energy equals power times time. Power in watts, times time in seconds, gives energy in joules.

steps.say: A 40 W lamp is on for 10 s. Energy = 40 × 10 = 400 J.
steps.speak: A 40 watt lamp is on for 10 seconds. Energy equals 40 times 10, which is 400 joules.

steps.say: The time must be in **seconds**. A 10 W lamp is on for 2 minutes. 2 minutes = 120 s, so energy = 10 × 120 = 1200 J.
steps.speak: The time must be in seconds. A 10 watt lamp is on for 2 minutes. 2 minutes is 120 seconds, so energy equals 10 times 120, which is 1200 joules.

steps.say: You can go the other way too: **power = energy ÷ time**. A hairdryer transfers 12,000 J in 10 s. Power = 12,000 ÷ 10 = 1200 W.
steps.speak: You can go the other way too: power equals energy divided by time. A hairdryer transfers 12,000 joules in 10 seconds. Power equals 12,000 divided by 10, which is 1200 watts.

check.q: A 20 W fan runs for 30 s. How much energy does it transfer?
check.hint: Energy = power × time. Multiply, don't add. And energy is measured in joules.
check.explain: Energy = 20 W × 30 s = **600 J**. Adding gives 50, which is wrong, and watts are for power, not energy.

steps.say: A home uses millions of joules every day. So energy companies use a much bigger unit of energy: the **kilowatt-hour**, **kWh**.
steps.speak: A home uses millions of joules every day. So energy companies use a much bigger unit of energy: the kilowatt-hour.

steps.say: 1 kWh is the energy a 1 kW device transfers in 1 hour. That is 3,600,000 J!
steps.speak: 1 kilowatt-hour is the energy a 1 kilowatt device transfers in 1 hour. That is 3.6 million joules!

steps.say: **Energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours**. A 2 kW heater on for 4 hours uses 2 × 4 = 8 kWh.
steps.speak: Energy in kilowatt-hours equals power in kilowatts times time in hours. A 2 kilowatt heater on for 4 hours uses 2 times 4, which is 8 kilowatt-hours.

steps.say: Change watts to kilowatts first. A 200 W TV is 0.2 kW. On for 5 hours, it uses 0.2 × 5 = 1 kWh.
steps.speak: Change watts to kilowatts first. A 200 watt TV is 0.2 kilowatts. On for 5 hours, it uses 0.2 times 5, which is 1 kilowatt-hour.

check.q: A 3 kW oven is on for 2 hours. How much energy does it use?
check.hint: kWh = kW × hours. The power is already in kW, so just multiply.
check.explain: 3 kW × 2 h = **6 kWh**. Don't add (5) or divide (1.5). The power is already in kW, so there is no need to multiply by 1000.

steps.say: You pay for every kWh you use. In our examples, electricity costs **25p for each kWh**.
steps.speak: You pay for every kilowatt-hour you use. In our examples, electricity costs 25 pence for each kilowatt-hour.

steps.say: **Cost = energy in kWh × price per kWh**. The heater used 8 kWh. 8 × 25p = 200p, which is £2.
steps.speak: Cost equals energy in kilowatt-hours times the price per kilowatt-hour. The heater used 8 kilowatt-hours. 8 times 25 pence is 200 pence, which is 2 pounds.

steps.say: An **electricity meter** counts the kWh a home uses. On Monday it reads 05120. On Friday it reads 05150. 5150 − 5120 = 30 kWh used.
steps.speak: An electricity meter counts the kilowatt-hours a home uses. On Monday it reads 5120. On Friday it reads 5150. 5150 minus 5120 is 30 kilowatt-hours used.

steps.say: So the cost from Monday to Friday is 30 × 25p = 750p, which is £7.50.
steps.speak: So the cost from Monday to Friday is 30 times 25 pence, which is 750 pence, or 7 pounds 50.

check.q: A meter reads 02400 kWh one week and 02420 kWh the next. Electricity costs 25p per kWh. What did that week's energy cost?
check.hint: First take the readings away to find the kWh used. Then multiply by 25p. Remember 100p = £1.

steps.say: How much energy a device uses depends on two things: its **power** and **how long** it is on.
A 2 kW hairdryer on for 15 minutes uses 2 × 0.25 = 0.5 kWh. A 100 W TV on for 5 hours uses 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 kWh. Exactly the same!
steps.speak: A 2 kilowatt hairdryer on for 15 minutes, which is a quarter of an hour, uses 2 times 0.25, which is 0.5 kilowatt-hours. A 100 watt TV on for 5 hours uses 0.1 times 5, which is 0.5 kilowatt-hours. Exactly the same!

steps.say: Ways to save energy: switch off lights and screens, use LED bulbs, have shorter showers, and turn the heating down a little.
Saving energy saves money. It can also mean less fuel is burned in power stations, which is better for the planet.

check.q: Which uses more energy: a 1 kW heater on for 3 hours, or a 2 kW heater on for 1 hour?
options: The 1 kW heater on for 3 hours
The 2 kW heater on for 1 hour
You can't tell without the price
check.hint: Work out kWh = kW × hours for each heater, then compare.
check.explain: 1 kW × 3 h = **3 kWh**. 2 kW × 1 h = 2 kWh. The smaller heater uses more, because it is on for much longer.
